編鐘採用體鳴方式發聲，撞擊後產生的共鳴悠長且富有餘韻，音波緩慢衰減，能營造莊嚴肅: The bianzhong sounds as an idiophone: struck, it rings long and full of aftertone, the sound waves fading slowly, which can set a solemn, grave atmosphere. Compared with modern wind instruments it seems older and more refined; compared with the Western glockenspiel its timbre has more of an Eastern flavour, and its bass is deeper and more powerful. Its sound has both the brilliance of a bronze instrument and the elegance of traditional court music, and in ancient palace music it created a particular kind of splendour.
編鐘為中國青銅時代以來的體鳴樂器，周代（前1046–前256）形成成組懸掛的編鐘: The bianzhong is an idiophone used in China since the Bronze Age; in the Zhou dynasty (1046–256 BC) sets of bells were hung together, and the set from the tomb of Marquis Yi of Zeng dates from about 430 BC. In the Qin and Tang periods the bells grew smaller, with one pitch per bell; from the Song dynasty the form settled as sixteen bells on a two-tier frame, which lasted into the Qing. In the Song dynasty bianzhong reached the Korean court, and the court at Huế in Vietnam used them too. After Zhou-dynasty bells were excavated in 1978, modern ensembles began playing reconstructed sets from the 1980s.

Its range is wide, spanning several octaves, so it can play melody and harmony. Each bell's timbre varies with its size: the large bells are low and full, the small ones high and crisp, and the layers are clearly marked.

It also reached Korea and Vietnam: in Korea it is used in ritual music, court music and the Confucian memorial rite, leading the ensemble and doubling the wind and string melody, with the large bells punctuating phrases of the hymn; Vietnamese court ritual used it as well. Today historical performance groups play reconstructed bianzhong at home and abroad.

The bianzhong is an ancient Chinese idiophone, Hornbostel-Sachs number 111.242.221, made up of bronze bells arranged by size and hung on a wooden frame, struck with mallets or sticks and able to play melody; some bells can sound two pitches depending on where they are struck. It belongs to the bell family and is often used with the stone chimes, and the metal in the phrase "the sound of metal and stone" means the bianzhong. From the Zhou dynasty it was a ritual vessel of the ruling class, used in sacrifice and court music, and it also reached Korea, Vietnam and Japan; Korean Confucian rites still use it today.
